questions.question: Define the mobile phase in GC and give examples. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define the mobile phase in GC and give examples. [U] / [CO2]
  • In gas chromatography (GC), the mobile phase is an inert gas, called the carrier gas that
  • transports the sample through the column. Common examples include helium, nitrogen, and
  • hydrogen. The carrier gas moves the analytes through the stationary phase, where they are
  • separated based on their different physical and chemical properties

questions.question: Define electrophoresis. Who pioneered the technique of electrophoresis? / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Define electrophoresis. Who pioneered the technique of electrophoresis.[K][CO5]
  • Electrophoresis is a laboratory technique that uses an electric field to move charged molecules in
  • a fluid or gel, separating them based on their size, charge, or binding affinity.  It is used to
  • separate and analyze molecules like DNA, RNA, and proteins. The Swedish biochemist  Arne
  • Tiselius pioneered the technique of electrophoresis in the 1930s

  • constant magnetic field are disturbed by a weak oscillating magnetic field and respond by
  • producing an electromagnetic signal with a frequency characteristic of the magnetic field at the
  • nucleus

questions.question: Explain the principle, working, and applications of paper chromatography. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the principle, working, and applications of chromatography paper [U] / [CO2]
  • Paper chromatography  separates a mixture based on its components' different solubilities and
  • affinities for the stationary and mobile phases.  The process involves a stationary phase of water
  • trapped in the paper and a mobile phase of a solvent that moves up the paper by capillary
  • action. Components of a mixture spotted on the paper are carried up by the solvent at different
  • rates, leading to their separation into distinct spots at different heights.  Applications include
  • separating inks, analyzing dyes in food, testing for drug doping, and identifying pigments in
  • plants

questions.question: Write briefly about differential, rate zonal, and isopycnic centrifugation methods. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Write briefly about differential, rate zonal, and isopycnic centrifugation methods.
  • [U] / [CO5]
  • Differential centrifugation: This technique separates particles primarily by size and density using
  • a series of increasing centrifugal forces. It is a simple and common method for initial purification
  • and isolating subcellular components.
  • Rate-zonal centrifugation separates particles by their sedimentation rate (size and shape), while
  • isopycnic centrifugation separates them by their buoyant density, independent of size.  Rate-zonal
  • uses a shallow gradient and shorter run times, best for separating particles that differ in size but
  • not density, like organelles.  Isopycnic uses a steep gradient and longer run times, ideal for
  • separating particles based on density.

questions.question: Describe the different modes of centrifugation. / [CO5] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the different modes of centrifugation. [U] / [CO5]
  • The main modes of centrifugation are differential centrifugation and density gradient
  • centrifugation, with the latter often broken down into rate zonal and isopycnic
  • techniques. Differential centrifugation separates components by spinning samples at increasing
  • speeds, while density gradient centrifugation separates based on density using a prepared
  • gradient medium, which can either be separated by speed (rate zonal) or by the density at which
  • components reach equilibrium (isopycnic)
  • [2x10 = 20]
